title: Design with materials, not features
principle: For open-ended creative software, don’t ship a bag of buttons for N tasks. Present materials with consistent laws of physics so users compose N×N capabilities.
procedure: Name the primary materials the user will manipulate (shapes, commits, clips, notes)—not the feature list.
Write the laws of physics: what can combine, collide, nest, or never occupy the same slot.
Prefer spatial/composable metaphors over deep menu hierarchies when tasks are open-ended.
Stress-test: can a user invent a workflow you didn’t design? If not, you still have a feature bag.
Cut features that don’t act on a material; fold them into tools that operate on materials.
examplePrompts:
Redesign this product as materials + laws of physics, not a feature menu.

Primary materials: <list>
Laws of physics: <what can combine / collide / nest>
Tasks that must remain possible: <list>
Do not add unrelated feature buttons. Show how each capability emerges from materials.
Compare two IA sketches: (A) feature-bag home with N buttons, (B) one canvas of materials with tools. Prefer B unless tasks are single-path. Explain tradeoffs in one paragraph.
promptWhy: Forces the model to invent composable primitives instead of menu sprawl.
Makes the feature-bag failure mode explicit before pixels.
tips: Linus: feature-bag apps fit well-defined paths (Uber, Search); material apps fit open creation (Figma, Notes, Git).
Git’s material is the commit—even without a spatial metaphor.

workedExamples.title: Figma vs Uber home
workedExamples.before: Home is a grid of feature buttons for every job.
workedExamples.after: Canvas of shapes/text with tools that operate on materials.
workedExamples.body: Linus contrasts Uber/Google (clear paths → features) with Figma/Notes/file explorers (open tasks → materials + physics). Cite materials essay.

workedExamples.title: Git as material
workedExamples.before: Version control as a menu of git commands.
workedExamples.after: Commits as the material; branches/tags as compositions of commits with strict rules.
workedExamples.body: Even without spatial UI, commits obey laws (order, diff, scope). Cite materials essay.

antiPatterns: Adding another top-level button for every new workflow.
Static mockups that freeze materials before you learn their physics in the medium.
checklist: Laws of physics are written and consistent.
At least one unforeseen workflow is possible.
Feature buttons that don’t act on materials are cut or folded.
